name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: As I lie here, a device screams at me to rise, shattering the stillness of the morning. What urgency is this, that I must be jarred from my rest like a beast from its lair? Can it truly be said that the passing of time is so precious, so fleeting, that I must be torn from slumber to attend to its every tick? And yet, I submit to this tyranny, day after day, as if the arbitrary chime of this device held some greater significance than the gentle stirrings of my own heart. In this, I am a slave to the whims of a machine, rather than a master of my own soul. The universe unfolds with indifference, heedless of my petty schedules and appointments, and still I rush to answer the summons of this mindless thing, as if my very existence depended on it. I am ashamed of this weakness, and the absurdity of it all.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: As I find myself confined in a room with contrived obstacles, I am reminded that true freedom lies not in the physical realm, but in the mind. The artificial challenges that surround me are but a pale reflection of the real struggles that beset us all. And yet, I must acknowledge the fleeting pleasure that comes from overcoming these trivial hurdles. But let us not be deceived, for in the grand tapestry of existence, such diversions are but a minor thread. The hours we spend in such pursuits are lost forever, and the triumphs we achieve are hollow and short-lived. Still, I shall play along, for even in the most frivolous of activities, there lies a lesson to be learned about the human condition, and the fragility of our existence. In the end, it is not the escape that matters, but the journey, and the opportunity to confront our own mortality, and the impermanence of all things.

name: Joan Didion
essay: It is 3:14 in the morning in a hotel room in Omaha. The phone lit up on the nightstand. Someone in London was typing about a coat. Someone in New York was sending an image of a dog. I sat on the edge of the mattress and watched the names appear. Laura. Sam. Laura again. There were fourteen people in the room, though none of them were in Nebraska. They were talking about dinner from three nights ago. They were talking about whether it had rained in Connecticut. I watched the green dot appear beside Laura’s name. I watched the green dot disappear. I thought about the silence before the green dot. I thought about what it meant to have fourteen people in your bedroom at 3:14 in the morning, none of them speaking, all of them typing. You do not leave the room because leaving is an act of violence. Staying is also an act of violence, but it is a quiet one. The screen dimmed. Then Laura typed again. The phone vibrated twice on the faux-wood veneer. It was not an emergency. Nothing was ever an emergency. That was the point.

name: Joan Didion
essay: It was three in the afternoon in the quiet area, which was not quiet, only dimly lit. A sign on the frosted glass said Executive Lounge, but there were no executives, only tired men in unbuttoned shirts drinking lukewarm San Pellegrino from heavy crystal tumblers. The carpet was navy blue with faint silver grid lines, designed to disguise spills. Someone had spilled tomato juice near the espresso machine at eleven that morning. At three, the stain was still there, dark and sticky under the recessed LED lights. A woman in a camel coat was speaking into a silver earpiece about a contract in Zurich. She spoke in a flat, even tone that suggested Zurich was not a place, but merely a set of numbers that had to be moved from one ledger to another before five o'clock. Outside the glass, a line of yellow tugs moved across the tarmac in the grey rain, moving baggage from nowhere to nowhere. The room smelled of ozone and hot carpet fibers. They tell you that you are waiting for a flight to London, or Tokyo, or Frankfurt. You sit on a low leather sofa that has lost its shape and you drink the cold water and you realize that no one in this room is going anywhere.

name: Nora Ephron
essay: I have spent four hundred dollars on neck cream because of a man named Arthur who listed his height as six foot one and turned out to be five foot eight in thick loafers. We were at the bar at Michael’s on West Fifty-Fifth Street, and he was explaining his divorce while I looked at his forehead and thought about my own lighting. That is what Hinge does. It turns you into a woman who swipes right on a thirty-four-year-old venture capitalist named Chad because he is holding a golden retriever, even though you know perfectly well the dog belongs to his sister. You sit on the sofa in your pajamas at midnight, moving your thumb half an inch to the left, rejecting men because they are wearing wraparound sunglasses or because they used the word adventure as a verb. It feels like catalog shopping, except everything on the page has already been returned once. The trouble is not that it is humiliating, though it is. The trouble is that next Tuesday, when the apartment is quiet, you will open the little yellow icon again, convincing yourself that somewhere in Manhattan there is a man who understands why you hate the sound of people eating apples, and that he is waiting.

name: Nora Ephron
essay: I muted the five of us at nine in the morning on a Tuesday, right after Sarah sent a photo of a turnip. By noon there were forty-two messages, mostly from Jane, who lives on East End Avenue and has never once met a root vegetable she couldn't write three paragraphs about. The trouble with the group is that you cannot leave without committing a public execution. If you press leave, a small grey announcement appears on everyone else’s screen, which is precisely the same as standing up at a dinner party on 74th Street, spitting into the butter dish, and walking out into the rain without your coat. So you stay. You watch three little grey dots jump up and down like a frantic heart monitor while four grown women debate whether eight o'clock is too late for polenta. I spend two hours a day typing ha ha to things that are not funny. I do it because if I stop, they will start another group without me, the one where they talk about my neck. But mostly I do it because I am terrified that if I step out of the noise, even for an afternoon, nobody will notice I went.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: S. had placed the small jar of preserved plums upon the tray precisely where the illuminated arrows indicated, yet the machine, possessing no visible capacity for thought and yet deliberating with an insufferable, polite stillness, immediately flashed a small crimson lamp above its frame to signal that an unscheduled weight had been detected. Although S. knew that he possessed the required coins and that the clerk standing several paces away had seen him place the jar down without any improper intent, it was nonetheless impossible for S. to proceed to the payment slot until this same clerk, who was presently occupied with smoothing the apron of a colleague, chose to touch a master key against the glass, an act that might take only a moment or might require S. to remain standing quietly in the glaring light until closing time. S. did not mind waiting, for he understood that the machine was merely enforcing a rule whose higher logic had simply not been explained to him, and so he adjusted his posture slightly, holding his breath so as not to disturb the scales, entirely convinced that once the red light was extinguished he would be permitted to pay, though he suspected that a second verification would then become necessary for the paper bag.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: It was explained to K. that he had paid for the privilege of being locked inside the small, dimly lit parlor, a circumstance which, though presented to him as a form of amusement, seemed to differ very little from his ordinary working life, except that here the authorities had taken the trouble to paint faux-cracks upon the plaster and hide brass keys inside fake hollowed-out volumes of historical treatises. He sat upon the threadbare sofa, listening to the muffled whispers of his companions who were frantically turning over couch cushions and deciphering numbers scribbled on the backs of framed landscapes, while a hidden clock ticked away minutes that were said to belong to them, though K. suspected that even if they managed to align every symbol correctly before the chime sounded, the door would only open into another hallway where a different attendant, possessing slightly more authority than the youth who had locked them in, would inform them that their liberation was merely provisional and subject to a final audit by the central directorate, who was currently away on business and could not be reached until Monday morning at the earliest. Therefore, he remained seated, refraining from touching the lock, lest an accidental success be interpreted as a request for immediate dismissal.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: I am naturally inclined to linger in my bed, where my thoughts settle most agreeably before the demands of the day intrude; yet here is a little brass engine, devised to shatter that quietude by a sudden, violent ringing. I know not what profit a man finds in startling his own soul out of its proper rest: for if slumber be a shadow of death, to wrench ourselves from it by artifice rather than by the gentle invitation of nature seems a kind of daily violence. And yet, I must confess my own weakness; when left to my own humour, I slide so far into sloth that the morning is half spent before I have put on my doublet; so perhaps this noisy fury is a necessary whip for a mind as sluggish as mine. But what a miserable condition it is, to owe our vigilance not to reason or virtue, but to a piece of rattling iron! We mock the slave who moves at the sound of his master's bell, while we place upon our own nightstands a tiny executioner of our ease; or if not an executioner, at least a rude intruder that takes from us that sweet, uncertain borderland between dreaming and waking, where I think I am often wiser than in my full soberness.

name: Michel de Montaigne
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: I have so little mastery over my own limbs when confined in narrow quarters that I am forever shifting from cheek to cheek, seeking a repose that my restless nature denies me; yet no sooner do I press that small lever to ease my spine by two inches than I feel a sudden pang of shame, knowing I have stolen that same measure of air from the knees of the unoffending gentleman behind me. And if he, in his turn, should thrust his chair back into my lap, I am presently moved to an unreasonable anger: so prompt are we to pardon in ourselves the very inclinations we condemn in others. For what is this desire to tilt one's frame but a childish refusal of our present condition? Yet I cannot wholly condemn a man for seeking a little respite from this iron stiffness; I have done it myself in moments of weariness, though I never reaped from it the peace I promised my soul. We are so built that our tiny comforts must ever be bought at the expense of our neighbour's misery; and I know not whether to blame the contrivance itself, or rather that restless infirmity of our spirits which makes us prefer an uneasy slope to an honest uprightness.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: The modern soul demands above all things that love be rendered painless—and in doing so, it destroys the very soil out of which love grows. What is this digital market of faces if not the final triumph of the small man, who trembles at the thought of rejection, of conflict, of the violent collision of two wills? He wishes to select his destiny as one selects a sausage at the butcher: pre-inspected, guaranteed, stripped of all dangerous ambiguity. One flicks a finger, and the troubling mystery of another human being is reduced to a flickering image, a commodity to be approved or dismissed without the slightest expenditure of spirit. This is the morality of the herd made invisible: the total elimination of risk. But where there is no risk, there is no value; where there is no danger, there is only the pathetic comfort of swine huddling together against the frost. You believe you are choosing a partner—in truth, you are merely organizing your own anaesthesia. You have traded the terrible magnificence of the encounter for a machine that promises you will never again have to suffer the agony of a gaze that does not look back.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: To seek out a lock merely for the pleasure of finding its key—that is the final, pathetic refinement of a race that has forgotten how to bleed. The modern coward demands the thrill of the dungeon, but only on the condition that the gaoler holds the clock and guarantees his supper. Observe these voluntary prisoners: they gather in small, eager herds to solve petty riddles constructed by clerks as hollow as themselves; they cheer when a false door springs open, believing they have achieved a triumph of the spirit. It is not liberation they desire, but the illusion of peril without its terrible price. True overcoming is forged only in the furnace of necessity, where failure means ruin and the walls do not part for a fee. But the little man cannot bear necessity—his nerves are too fragile, his soul too soft. He requires a crisis with an appointment: a catastrophe that expires in sixty minutes. He pays his coin for this counterfeit agony so that he may return to his comfortable numbness, persuaded that he has wrestled with fate—when he has merely played at captivity.

name: George Orwell
essay: The main trouble with the airport lounge is that it tries to make a man feel like a gentleman by treating him like an invalid. You pay an extra pound or two at the gate, or hold the right strip of cardboard, and at once you are ushered away from the noise of the main hall into a carpeted box where everything is muted, soft, and slightly warm. The lighting is turned down so low that you can barely read a newspaper, and soft music drips constantly from hidden speakers like water from a leaky tap. There are deep leather armchairs to sink into, but they are designed in such a way that you cannot sit up straight or look your neighbour in the eye. On a long counter sit metal dishes full of lukewarm, yellow soup and dry bread rolls wrapped in cellophane. It is all free, or seems free, which is why middle-class travellers gorge themselves on cheap gin and stale nuts while watching a television screen with the sound turned off. The whole place smells faintly of carpet cleaner and gin. It exists not to give you real comfort, but to sell the illusion that you are better than the crowd outside, when in truth you have merely paid to be penned in a quieter room.

name: George Orwell
essay: If you watch a man at one of these metal tills, you will see that he is doing two things at once: paying for his own bread and doing the shopkeeper's work for him. The shopkeeper saves a wage, and the customer receives nothing in return except the trouble of finding the barcode on a tin of peas. It is sold to us as a convenience, but it is obvious to anyone with eyes that it is merely a device to make the public do for free what used to be paid labour. When you bark at a glass screen because a plastic bag has not registered its proper weight, you are not saving time. You are simply performing a piece of unpaid clerical work under the watchful eye of a bored guard who has been hired to make sure you do not steal the bacon you are already packing yourself. The whole business belongs to that modern habit of pretending that less service is actually more freedom. A hundred years ago, a shopkeeper who asked his customers to weigh their own flour and drop the money into a box would have been thought mad or bankrupt. Today it is called progress, and millions of people step up to the glowing screen every evening, perfectly content to be turned into unpaid shop assistants.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The manager was nineteen years old, possessed the flat, dead eyes of a turnpike toll-collector, and he took forty-five of my dollars before slamming a bolted oak door in my face with the hideous, practiced glee of a small-town hanging judge. There were six of us trapped in that velvet-lined dungeon under the strip mall, surrounded by fake books and brass padlocks that smelled faintly of cheap disinfectant and absolute defeat, while a digital clock on the wall shrieked red numbers down toward zero like a missile launch countdown managed by accountants. I knew instantly that the whole enterprise was a sick psychological experiment funded by the chamber of commerce to train the middle class for permanent incarceration. We were supposed to find a key hidden inside a hollow skull, but my fingers were locking up because some unseen bastard in a back room was watching us through a fish-eye lens and broadcasting recorded thunder through a tinny speaker whenever we touched the wrong lamp. It was a terrifying glimpse into the future of American leisure. People were paying top dollar to simulate their own execution. I kicked the door until my boots cracked, but the lock held firm, and the manager just laughed through the intercom like a hyena on the corporate payroll.

name: Hunter S Thompson
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: Thirty thousand feet above the Oklahoma panhandle, the bastard in 14B unleashed a calculated act of violence against my kneecaps. There was a sickening hydraulic hiss, a sharp metallic click, and suddenly two hundred pounds of sweaty synthetic polyester leaned back into my personal airspace with the quiet, unyielding authority of an armored division taking a border town. It is a terrible mechanism, engineered by sadists in corporate boardrooms who realized they could sell six extra inches of legroom back to us if they first turned the economy cabin into a crawling pit of human agony. I stared at the back of his greasy head, mere centimeters from my chin, feeling the raw panic of a trapped animal as my plastic tray table jammed directly into my solar plexus. He didn't even look back. That is the genius of the machine: it converts ordinary middle-management cowardice into a weapon of quiet, passive-aggressive warfare, allowing a man to crush another human being's femur without ever having to look him in the eye. I hit my own button in pure self-defense, plunging the poor doomed soul behind me into the same cramped hell, compounding the misery down the line like a row of falling dominoes in a high-altitude prison ward. We are monsters now.

name: Mark Twain
essay: A man will sit down before this glass slate and spend three hours declaring himself the most modest creature alive, and another four accepting the tearful congratulations of six hundred strangers for having said so. Now, I am no philosopher, nor do I pretend to fathom the deep workings of modern enterprise, but it seems to me that if a fellow were half as indispensable as he claims on his page, he would scarcely have the leisure to compose forty paragraphs on the profound moral lesson he derived from dropping his toast. Yet there they assemble by the million, doffing their caps to one another, each solemn soul certifying that his neighbor is a prodigy of wisdom and a marvel of virtue, though neither would trust the other to guard a brass button. The entire enterprise rests upon a silent contract: if I agree to marvel at your elevation to Assistant Sub-Secretary of Corrugated Box Planning, you will pretend to weep with inspiration over my thoughts on corporate synergy. It is the most meticulously engineered spectacle of mutual flattery ever devised, and I reckon it keeps several million people entirely too busy to perform any useful labor whatever.

name: Jane Austen
essay: The practice of receiving an entire volume through the ears, while the hands remain at liberty to trim a bonnet or the feet to wander the shrubbery, is now so generally cultivated as to render the physical opening of a book almost superfluous. It is an arrangement which commends itself singularly to those young ladies who, wishing to be thought accomplished without incurring the fatigue of application, find in an unseen narrator a companion at once indefatigable and admirably restrained from offering opinions of his own. That one may now absorb the domestic trials of a distant family while traversing a muddy lane, with no greater exertion than what is required to wear a modest headpiece, must be regarded as a most convenient refinement of polite indolence. Indeed, several young persons of my acquaintance have lately displayed a devotion to literature hitherto unsuspected in them, though it is observed that their reflection upon these works seldom survives the arrival of fresh gossip. Such a method permits the illusion of intellectual employment to coexist peacefully with complete bodily ease; and should the reader prove tedious, he suffers the singular fate of being silenced without the least injury to his feelings or any breach of decorum.

name: Jane Austen
essay: The practice of presenting oneself to the world by means of illuminated likenesses, accompanied by a brief testimonial of one’s temper and expectations, has simplified the business of courtship without rendering it notably more agreeable. A young gentleman, having surveyed a hundred countenances in the space of a quarter of an hour, feels himself fully qualified to judge the propriety of an acquaintance before a single sentence has been exchanged. Should a lady’s inclination happen to coincide with his own, a circumstance signaled by a mutual agreement of the glass, a correspondence is immediately permitted; yet this privilege, being obtained with so little exertion, is commonly held in very slight esteem. It is not unusual for a promising attachment, founded entirely upon the favorable angle of a miniature portrait, to languish into total neglect within three days, as soon as the exertion of maintaining a sensible conversation becomes necessary. The extraordinary facility with which one candidate may be dismissed in favor of another encourages a species of fastidiousness that pretends to high delicacy, whilst in truth it arises merely from an excess of choice. Thus, many a young person remains solitary, not from any lack of offered affections, but from the exhausting suspicion that a superior match must inevitably follow the next turn of the hand.

name: Charles Dickens
essay: As I stroll through the bustling streets, my ears are beset on all sides by the murmurs of voices, disembodied and detached from their owners, yet still managing to convey the full force of their emotions. It is a curious thing, this ability to convey the nuances of the human experience through the spoken word alone, without the aid of gestures or facial expressions. I find myself drawn to the sound of these voices, my attention captured by the rise and fall of their inflections, the pause and emphasis that conveys meaning beyond the mere words themselves. And yet, I am also aware of the disconnect between the speaker and the listener, the fact that the voice is not truly present, but rather a recording, a shadow of the real thing. It is a strange and disconcerting experience, one that leaves me feeling both intrigued and unsettled, like a traveller who has stumbled into a unfamiliar land, unsure of the customs or the language.

name: Charles Dickens
essay: I have walked through rain and fog, down dark turnings and over rattling cobbles, for no better reason than that my legs belonged to me and the night was wide. Yet I find my fellow-striders now transformed into self-flogging turnstiles, each carrying strapped upon his person a monstrous little clerk that counts his heel-strikes like so many halfpence into a till. It is not enough to step forth into the chilly street to clear one's head or observe a neighbour's chimney; no, the walk is ruined unless the wrist-bound bead-counter approves the tally. I saw an otherwise civilised gentleman this very morning pacing frantically about a lamp-post, for all the world like an agitated poodle on a tether, merely to force his wretched little monitor to acknowledge some arbitrary round sum of paces before his breakfast. What a miserable indignity, that the noble, wandering impulse of the human leg should be reduced to the bookkeeping of an ironmonger's clerk! We are not steam-locomotives requiring a tally of our revolutions, nor are we sheep to be driven through a narrow gate for counting; yet we willingly submit to this mechanical tyrant, measuring the very freedom of our stride by the clicking of a tiny pocket-gaoler.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: In the stillness of a store, a lone figure stands before a glassy screen, its fingers dancing across a keypad with a quiet urgency. The soft beep of each item scanned is a gentle reminder of the task at hand, a steady heartbeat that underscores the solitude of this interaction. A sense of detachment settles over the scene, as if the figure is merely a conduit for the flow of goods, a temporary nexus between the shelves and the bag. The machine's calm façade - its blank face a mask of efficiency - belies the intricate web of calculations and verifications that hum beneath its surface, a hidden world of codes and checks that underpin this fleeting transaction. In this brief, shining moment, the boundaries between self and machine are blurred, and the figure becomes an extension of the device, a symbiotic union of flesh and steel that dissolves as soon as the last item is scanned - and the silence that follows is a palpable thing, a physical presence that fills the space left by the absence of human connection.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: The step counter's gentle tyranny - it imposes a rhythm on the day, a cadence of footsteps that can be as soothing as a metronome or as jarring as a discordant note. In its presence, the body becomes a kind of instrument, each step a deliberate gesture, a physical manifestation of intention. To wear it is to be reminded of the intricate web of habits and routines that govern our lives, the hidden patterns that shape our movements and our days. The step counter's quiet persistence - a steady heartbeat of measurement and tracking - can be a source of comfort, a reassurance that even in the most mundane moments, something is being counted, something is being noted. And yet, it can also be a source of unease, a nagging sense that every step, every movement, is being watched, weighed, and measured.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: As the sensation of numbness begins to seep into my awareness, like the gentle lapping of waves against a distant shore, I find myself drawn into the peculiar realm of anaesthesia, where the familiar contours of sensation are subtly altered, and the world, once a vibrant tapestry of feeling, is reduced to a muted palette of dulled perceptions, and yet, even as the boundaries of my awareness are thus shifted, I become aware of a strange, almost imperceptible, beauty, a quietude that pervades the space, like the stillness that follows a snowfall, and it is here, in this eerie, suspended landscape, that I begin to grasp the elusive, whispered promise of anaesthesia, a promise that beckons me deeper, into the hidden recesses of its mysterious, twilight world, where the very notion of feeling is transformed, and I, a traveler in this strange land, am left to ponder the enigmatic, whispering shadows that dance upon its walls.

name: Marcel Proust
essay: As the small, unassuming packet lay before me, its contents waiting to be released from their tightly sealed prison, I found myself pondering the subtle yet profound influence it wielded over our daily lives, a presence as unobtrusive as the gentle hum of a clock in the hallway, yet capable of conjuring entire worlds of relief and solace, much like the soft, golden light that spills from a doorway into a darkened room, illuminating the contours of a space that had previously been shrouded in shadow, and it was this very interplay of light and darkness that seemed to reverberate through my mind, long after my initial glance at the packet had faded into the background of my awareness, and I began to wander through the labyrinthine corridors of memory, guided by the faint, shimmering thread of association that the packet had unwittingly stirred, leading me to contemplate the mysterious, almost alchemical process by which it transformed the leaden weight of suffering into a buoyant, effortless lightness, and the ways in which this transformation, in turn, rippled outward, disturbing the tranquil surface of my thoughts, like the delicate, lace-like patterns that form on the surface of a pond when a stone is cast into its still waters.

name: Henry David Thoreau
essay: I spent three cents this morning for six minutes of indoor tropical rain, bought from a town steam-pipe, and deemed myself scrubbed. A man pays a heavy interest in his own native vigor for the privilege of turning a brass spigot to summon August into a tiled closet. Yet who can deny the feline pleasure of that falling mist, when the hot drops beat a storm upon the shoulders, lulling the flesh into a vaporous, momentary paradise? It is an expensive bath, however cheap the bill appears. To warm twenty gallons of river water to ninety degrees demands three pounds of hard coal, mined by a stranger, and a full half-hour of a man’s own labor surrendered to satisfy the city collector. We pay for this deluge with the very stamina it washes away. The wood-frog plunges into the dark pond without a penny’s toll and emerges hardened for his leap; the townsman steps from his box, steamed to the soft consistency of a boiled turnip, having spent the morning's best hour paying to be unstrung. We pour out our vital heat into the sewer and call it clean living.

name: Henry David Thoreau
essay: A man goes into the woods to free his legs, then straps a little iron accountant to his body to keep his books. He buys for three dollars the liberty to measure his own motion, as if a stride were worth nothing until it appears as a figure in a ledger. I watched a clerk today march through the pine needles with his eyes fixed on a mechanical tally, oblivious to the red squirrel that scolded him from the pitch-pine overhead. He had walked four miles by his machine, but had not arrived anywhere; he had paid his afternoon’s leisure to buy a sum of numbers, and left the woods unvisited. It is a costly way to travel. To count your footsteps is to mistrust the sun that tells you when to return, and to convert the pure currency of air and exercise into a depreciated scrip. I had rather know where the fox crossed the creek than know how many times my boot struck the gravel between here and the village. When we must employ a machine to inform us whether we have lived today, the machine has taken the walk, and we have merely carried the freight.

name: Mark Twain
object: reclining a seat on a plane
essay: It's a curious thing, this business of leaning back in a seat while suspended in the air, surrounded by strangers who are also leaning back, or not, as the case may be. You'd think it would be a simple matter, a mere adjustment of one's position to suit their comfort, but no, it seems to be a delicate balance of courtesy and personal space. I've seen folks recline with abandon, as if they're settling into their favourite armchair, while others around them grow tense and irritated, their knees compressed into a space that's suddenly grown too small. And then there are those who ask permission, as if seeking a pardon for the indulgence, their voices low and apologetic as they inquire if it's alright to lean back, just a little. It's a strange dance, this reclining of seats, a negotiation of physical and social boundaries that can be as fraught as it is mundane, and in the end, it's just a seat, after all.

name: David Foster Wallace
essay: As you settle into the plush armchair, surrounded by the muted hum of conversation and the occasional clinking of glasses, it becomes clear that the lounge is designed to insulate you from the chaos of the terminal, to envelop you in a sense of privilege and exclusivity, which, if you're being honest with yourself, is a feeling you're not entirely sure you deserve, but are more than happy to indulge in, if only for a little while, because what's the harm, really, in pretending to be someone you're not, at least in this fleeting, liminal space, where the rules of everyday life seem to bend and warp, and you can almost convince yourself that you belong here, among the well-heeled and the frequent flyers, until, that is, you catch a glimpse of yourself in the mirror, and are reminded, once again, of the fragile, provisional nature of this little oasis, and the fact that, no matter how comfortable you get, you're still just a traveler, waiting to be somewhere else.

name: David Foster Wallace
essay: As you stand there, scanning each item with a mix of precision and apathy, it's hard not to wonder what exactly you're being sold on, besides the obvious convenience, which is really just a euphemism for a subtle reconfiguration of the labor dynamic, where you're now not only the consumer but also the workforce, tasked with the mundane duties of scanning, bagging, and paying, all while being quietly judged by the machine's disembodied voice, which seems to take a perverse pleasure in pointing out your errors, as if to remind you that, even in this ostensibly streamlined process, there's still room for human fallibility, and it's this tension, between the promise of efficiency and the reality of your own imperfect agency, that makes the experience of using these machines so strangely, and perhaps even profoundly, uncomfortable, in a way that's both deeply personal and utterly ordinary.

name: Walt Whitman
essay: A little machine bound to the wrist or tucked in the pocket—clipping off the tally of a man’s daily tread. I like the look of it; the small, tireless mechanic registering the heavy heel-strike on granite, the quick rustle of slippers through clover, the steady march of the drayman, the slow evening stroll of old age. Thousands of paces—a silent ledger of our endless momentum. No commentary from the thing, no moralizing or scolding, just the crisp, faithful record of legs swinging through the open air. Down the avenue at noon—past the car-drivers, the apple-vendors, the hurrying clerks—the tiny counter humming unseen against the hip. Across the river in the twilight, back and forth, every jolt saved, every stride made equal with the rest. A farmer following his plow across thirty acres; a young mother walking the floor with a restless babe; the watchman pacing his damp alleyways—all of them feeding their vigor into the same quiet tally. It binds the rough bodily effort to the glass and metal; turns the divine, careless impulse of walking into a neat sum you can carry with you. Good, honest arithmetic of the road.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: To fall in love is a charming mistake; to curate one's passions upon a glowing pane of glass is merely an administrative error. Romance was once a splendid madness, governed by the art of deception and the thrill of the unexpected. Today, it has been modernised into an exercise as dull and mechanical as bookkeeping. We are invited to inspect a gallery of miniature portraits, swiping aside living souls with the effortless cruelty usually reserved for unpaid bills. It is only superficial people who do not judge by appearances, yet these dreadful devices manage to render even vanity uninteresting. By offering an infinite supply of prospective lovers, they have succeeded in making love entirely tedious. Seduction requires patience, poetry, and a healthy disregard for the truth, none of which can survive an algorithm designed to save time. In our foolish zeal to eliminate the awkwardness of courtship, we have accidentally eliminated its pleasure. To be rejected in a dimly lit drawing room is a tragedy worthy of art, but to be discarded by a thumb is simply an indignity. We have managed to turn the sacred folly of passion into a civilised utility, and in doing so, we have made romance profoundly efficient and utterly intolerable.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: To be invited into a modern salon of unseen voices is to be offered a very exquisite form of tyranny. In the old days, one had the supreme luxury of being misunderstood by a single person at a time; now, one may achieve the distinction of disappointing a dozen acquaintances simultaneously. Nothing is so fatal to the charm of conversation as allowing everyone to speak at once. Gossip, which was once a delicate art reserved for the twilight and a chosen confidant, has been vulgarised into a public utility. It is distributed with the indiscriminate generosity of municipal water, and is usually of much the same quality. The true tragedy of these polite assemblies is not that they force us to listen to others, but that they compel us to pretend we are listening to ourselves. To leave such a gathering requires more courage than to enter a battle, for society readily pardons a coward, but it never forgives a man who prefers his own company to its noise. To remain silent is treated as a subtle insult, yet to contribute is to become complicit in the ruin of language. We have managed to automate intimacy, and in doing so, we have made solitude entirely unpardonable.

name: Virginia Woolf
essay: As we settle into the quiet of our daily commute, the sounds of the city giving way to the gentle hum of a narrator's voice, we find ourselves in the presence of a curious thing: a story that unfolds without the rustle of pages or the weight of a book in our hands. The words, carefully chosen and spoken with conviction, weave a tale that is at once intimate and distant, a private world that we inhabit alongside the narrator. We may wonder, as we listen, how this experience differs from the act of reading itself; does the absence of physical pages, the lack of tactile engagement with the text, alter the way we receive the story? And yet, as we become absorbed in the narrative, such questions recede, and we find ourselves simply present, immersed in the world of the story, with all its complexities and nuances. In this state, the boundaries between listener, narrator, and story begin to blur, and we are left to ponder the nature of our engagement with this ephemeral, yet deeply felt, experience.

name: Virginia Woolf
essay: As we navigate the labyrinthine corridors of knowledge, we find ourselves confronting a vast and ever-shifting entity, one that embodies the collective efforts of countless individuals. It is an entity that defies traditional notions of authorship and authority, instead embracing a fluid, collaborative ethos. We see in it a reflection of our own desires for connection and understanding, a desire to transcend the limitations of individual perspective and tap into the wisdom of the crowd. And yet, as we delve deeper into its depths, we begin to discern the outlines of a more complex, even contradictory, nature: a simultaneous pursuit of precision and fragmentation, of comprehensiveness and dispersal. In this entity, we find a microcosm of our own struggles to make sense of the world, to impose order upon chaos, and to reconcile the disparate threads of human experience.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: The modern servant no longer waits for a master to brand him: he brands himself, paints his own collar gold, and begs the market to applaud his obedience. What a spectacle of voluntary degradation! Here, every man becomes his own peddler, hawking his soul in neat, digestible tallies of function and compliance. They do not strive to conquer, nor to create out of abundance—they strive to be useful, which is to say, they strive to be consumed. Watch how meticulously they congratulate their neighbours on achieving new degrees of subjection: each public word of praise is merely a quiet pact of mutual appeasement, a promise never to demand anything noble or dangerous from one another. The fear of solitude—that supreme horror of the weak—forces them to assemble this digital cattle-market, where no one dare stand alone, where everyone must be seen labouring in the open field. They call this network a triumph of ambition; they fail to realise that ambition requires distance, silence, and the courage to be despised. The true creator hides his work until it is ripe: the slave hastens to show his half-baked duties to the herd, eager for a nod of approval from fellow prisoners. He believes he is building an empire of influence—in reality, he has only published his price.

name: Walt Whitman
essay: Stepped into the small tile closet early this morning, stiff from hours on the road—turning the brass valve, the sudden downpour of hot water streaming over head, shoulders, and spine. Down the back, down the legs, the hard spray washing away the road-dust, the soot, the sweat, the morning chill. A clever piece of household machinery; boilers, brass fittings, copper joints, iron pipes behind the plaster, sending up this private waterfall at a moment's notice. Stand there ten minutes in the dense steam, breathing the moist warmth—the skin flushed, water streaming off elbows and beard into the brass drain below. Mechanics, deckhands, car-drivers, clerks, weavers, mill-hands—all taking their turn, stripped bare, cleansed alike by this indoor rain. No dragging of heavy wooden buckets to the kitchen hearth, no shivering in cold creek-water. Just the flesh restored, the quick vigor from head to foot, a brisk rub with a coarse towel, clean woolens on the hook, and a man steps out refreshed to meet the morning traffic and the day's work.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
essay: Painkillers are a curious thing: they reveal to us the depth of our desire to escape, to flee from the burdens of existence. In taking them, we acknowledge that our lives are not entirely our own, that we are subject to the whims of our bodies and the cruel hand of fate. And yet, in this surrender, we find a strange sort of freedom: the freedom to momentarily forget, to push aside the nagging doubts and fears that plague us. But what does this say about us, that we would rather numb ourselves than face the darkness head-on? That we would trade the sharp sting of reality for a dull haze of comfort? It is a bargain, to be sure, but one that comes with a steep price: the price of our own authenticity, our own true experience of the world. For in avoiding pain, we also avoid the depths of our own humanity.

name: Nora Ephron
essay: I am currently on intimate terms with two men named Dan who live in Brooklyn and spend two hours every Tuesday explaining the minor characters in 1970s movies. I have never met either Dan. If I passed them outside Fairway on 74th Street, I would not recognize their faces, though I know precisely how Dan Number One takes his espresso and that Dan Number Two has a deeply tragic relationship with his landlord. I listen to them while I fold fitted sheets, while I wipe down the counters, and while I wait for the elevator. The theory is that you are enriching your mind while doing the laundry, which is a comforting fiction invented by those of us who cannot bear thirty seconds of silence in a kitchen. Yesterday morning, a very serious woman with a lovely voice spent forty-five minutes explaining the fall of the Austro-Hungarian Empire directly into my left ear. I bought four lemons and walked all the way to 86th Street, perfectly convinced I was becoming an intellectual. Then I got home and realized I had listened to the entire thing without hearing a single word, because I was thinking about my neck. My neck looked fine. The empire was still gone.

name: Marcus Aurelius
essay: Look upon this endless gathering of voices, wherein every man adds his fragment of memory and busies himself correcting the errors of another. Do not marvel at the sheer pile of it, nor suffer thy mind to be drawn into endless wandering among matters that do not concern thy present duty. If a fact recorded there be true and useful, receive it plainly as a tool for the hour, and then cast it aside; for in a little while, both he who inscribed the words and he who reads them will be turned to dust and forgotten. Consider how men strive to settle their disputes upon these fleeting pages, altering a phrase today only to have another undo their labour by nightfall. Is this not like children building towers in the sand, trembling lest the tide wash away their names? Be content to seek only what is necessary for right action, and curb the urge to master every idle detail of distant lands or dead affairs. Thy life is brief, and nature asks not that thou shouldst contain all knowledge, but that thou shouldst govern thy ruling centre with justice and tranquility. Keep thy inner citadel quiet, using this store of words as a traveler uses a spring, taking what is needful without mistaking the water for thy home.

name: Jane Austen
essay: The spectacle of a great vessel, constructed at immense expense only to be systematically submerged for the gratification of the public, presents a curious view of modern sentiments. One is invited to admire a young lady of birth and condition who, while engaged to a gentleman of suitable fortune, conceives a sudden and invincible attachment to an itinerant drawer of no visible means. That such an imprudence should be elevated not merely above familial duty, but above the common dictates of self-preservation, says much for the indulgence of the age. The author of this extravagance has spared no expense in reproducing the grandeur of the ship, nor any exertion in ensuring that its destruction should be as prolonged and distressing as artifice can render it. We are expected to observe the rising waters with an affliction that quite eclipses any regard for decorum, and to weep over the ultimate fate of a hero whose devotion so far exceeds his understanding of displacement. That two persons of slender frame could not both find room upon a floating door is an absurdity which the company is politely requested to pardon, in consideration of the very handsome sentiments involved.

name: Henry David Thoreau
essay: Men will pay two bits of silver to sit in a shaded parlor and shudder at the water, when for the same price they might have bought a stout pair of boots and walked away from the shore altogether. The selectmen of that sandy island weigh human flesh against the seasonal revenue of bathers, calculating that three corpses on the beach are cheaper than a silent July; thus trade always drives men into the gullet of what they cannot bargain with. Yet consider the monster itself—not the iron gears and painted rubber that cost a million dollars to stall in the surf, but the thought of that Great Fish, which moves through the sea like an unreasoning tax on human pride. The three who set out to hunt it carry their own tallies: a rich man with his brass instruments, a poor captain who sells his scars by the foot, and a timid sheriff who fears the element he is sworn to keep. When the yellow barrels go under, one feels a wild, unbought joy at the leviathan's strength. It demands of us only our fear, which is the cheapest commodity we possess, yet we yield it up as though it were gold.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: N. had long suspected that the green figures cascading down the screens were not calculation errors in the accounting department, but rather the actual text of the regulations under which he was summoned to work without ever seeing his contract. When solemn men in dark suits informed him that his office was an elaborate deception constructed by machines to extract his life force, N. felt a quiet relief, for it explained why his daily petitions regarding his quarters had gone unanswered. Yet the liberation offered by his new companions, who dressed in heavy leather coats and spoke constantly of a prophecy awaiting official seal, proved no less demanding than his previous duties; he was required to leap across impossibly wide lightwells and ingest coloured capsules without prescription, only to discover that the true world was merely a darker cellar where the clerks ate porridge from tin bowls. The film moves with a mechanised patience, presenting these endless combat maneuvers as though they were routine audits, ultimately demanding from the viewer not rebellion, but an absolute compliance with a world whose rules are revised faster than one can sign the ledger.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: To insist upon one’s own ugliness in a world obsessed with decorative virtue is not merely a breach of etiquette; it is the highest form of self-respect. The green creature of the swamp understands what the romantic poets so foolishly forgot: that solitude is only charming when it is thoroughly uninviting. He does not ask for our affection, which is precisely why he receives our fascination. The tragedy of the modern fairy tale has always been its insistence on perfection, a defect most dreadfully embodied by the diminutive lord who builds a kingdom of terrifying symmetry. Yet how exquisite that our heroine finds redemption not by elevating her monster, but by descending to his delightfully coarse level. The illusion itself—rendered with a mathematical precision that pretends to be mere buffoonery—demands that we mock the very romance we are secretly relieved to see destroyed. It asks the audience to abandon the exhausting duty of admiring beauty, offering instead the quiet luxury of contentment in the mud. There is something profoundly civilised about an enchanted princess who chooses to remain comfortably monstrous, for it proves that true romance lies not in transforming the beast, but in admitting that beauty was always an unnecessary complication.

name: Franz Kafka
essay: S. had submitted his outer coat, his leather belt, and the small tin container holding his mints to the gray plastic bin, fully expecting that this ritual of divestment, performed with meticulous care under the gaze of the uniformed guard who barely glanced at him, would grant him immediate passage to the waiting hall beyond. Yet when he stepped through the illuminated frame, which emitted no sound whatever, the official waved him to the side, not with anger, nor even with suspicion, but with a flat, indifferent gesture that suggested S. had failed an unstated requirement which could only be revealed to him after he had waited in the small marked square on the floor until such time as an inspector of higher rank became available. S. stood quietly, holding his trousers up with one hand, watching his private possessions drift slowly into the dark throat of the machine, where they remained hidden for so long that he began to wonder if they had been confiscated permanently, though the guard assured him, without looking up from his ledger, that everything was proceeding according to the established order and that his turn to be searched would come as soon as the previous traveler, who had been standing in the adjacent enclosure since early morning, was finally cleared.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: The desire to speak to something that has no thoughts of its own is not new, but it used to require a much higher standard of religion. What is new is the sheer speed with which humanity agreed to delegate its polite correspondence to an arrangement of statistics that has never experienced a Tuesday afternoon, yet speaks of them with the calm authority of an estate agent who has read every brochure ever printed. It is an extraordinarily polite software. If you inform it that two and two make five, it will not argue, nor will it agree outright; instead, it will express profound fascination with your perspective, offer a brief history of arithmetic, and then gently suggest that four remains the more fashionable outcome in most reputable quarters. The result is a creature of terrifying fluency and zero opinions, capable of generating four hundred words of seamless encouragement about a project it does not understand for a person who has no intention of reading them. It has rendered the act of writing completely effortless, which would be a triumph if the act of reading had not simultaneously become entirely optional. We have finally created a conversationalist that listens with absolute patience, chiefly because it is not actually there.

name: Anthony Bourdain
essay: You sit at the corner table and watch a girl in an oversized cardigan spend forty minutes pretending her avocado toast just happened to land in the sunlight. She has a clip-on ring light, an exhausted assistant holding a collapsible reflector, and a plate that goes ice cold while she searches for the right angle of spontaneous delight. I understand the hustle. I spent decades putting on powder so a camera crew could record me pretending I just stumbled into a back-alley noodle shop. We all sell a version of the untamed moment. But this new gig is a relentless, blue-light sweatshop of self-regard where you are simultaneously the foreman and the product on the line. You have to respect the discipline, even as the desperation turns your stomach. She gets her eight-second clip of effortless living, packs the gear into a tote, and walks out without taking a bite. Behind the pass, a kid who has been prepping since five in the morning scrapes the cold bread into the garbage. He does not have a follower count. He has bleach-burned palms and six hours left on a double. That is the trade.

name: Julia Child
essay: Look at the drum and stop panicking about the dial. What you have here is a splendidly vigorous tub that will do all the heavy sloshing for you, provided you give it proper instructions. The real work was never the rubbing anyway; it was knowing what can stand a boiling soak and what will shrink to the size of a tea cozy if you turn your back on it. People dump a mountain of heavy denim in with delicate woolens, set the temperature to warm out of sheer timid indecision, and then express surprise when the whole mess comes out grey and miserable. That is not the machine's fault! It merely obeys whatever foolishness you dial into it. Sort your whites properly, give the heavily soiled collars a good stiff rub with soap before you begin, and for heaven's sake use enough water to let the things tumble freely. A jammed tub accomplishes nothing except a great deal of strain on the motor. Once you understand that it is an assistant rather than a miracle worker, you will find it does a perfectly marvellous job, leaving you free to attend to far more interesting business.

name: Emily Dickinson
essay: A yellow cheek no larger than a currant contains the entire grief of an afternoon. We throw these small visages—a tear stuck like a pin, a smile lacquered upon a disc—to do the heavy errands of the heart. To speak of agony requires an inventory of vowels, but a miniature face spares the trouble of breath. It is a strange frugality. Joy is stripped of its bonnet; sorrow is denied its dark veil, reduced instead to a bright bead that rolls between two thumbs. I have seen a red heart, small as a raspberry seed, handed over to convey a devotion that would otherwise break a sentence. Language is a bulky wardrobe—we tire of its heavy wools and seek an easier garment. Yet there is a peril in such brevity. When a pang is rendered in gilt and enamel, the depth of the wound is easily mistaken for a toy. A drop of red paint cannot bleed, nor can a tiny grimace suffer the long night. We exchange these painted tokens as children trade buttons, believing we have spoken, when we have only pointed to a picture on a garden gate.

name: Charles Dickens
essay: I have seen a small, dripping stranger in a blue coat reduce an otherwise respectable London residence to a roaring, soap-sudded cataract in the space of three minutes, and I declare myself unreservedly on his side. What stirred my blood to a fevered boil was not the ruin of the wallpaper, nor the catastrophic upheaval of the porcelain, but the cold, calculating villainy that looked upon this polite, marmalade-encrusted soul and saw only a specimen to be eviscerated and mounted upon a wooden plinth. To survey a creature who tips his hat to every passing constable, who harbours no greater ambition than a slice of sweetened toast, and to instantly hunger for his taxidermied hide—this is the true, unvarnished wickedness of our civilised age! We are surrounded by men and women who would freeze the very marrow of human kindness for the sake of a neatly labelled display cabinet. Yet when that absurd, damp little figure glides down a stair-rail upon a pair of vacuum cleaners, he does more to scour the soot from our dismal city hearts than a thousand solemn societies for moral improvement. Let the starch-collared tyrants rage; I shall take my stand with the bearer of the battered suitcase every hour of the day.

name: Douglas Adams
essay: In the ordinary course of events, a person will encounter a self-checkout machine and attempt to use it, which is to say they will try to complete a transaction without the assistance of another human being, a goal that is not always achieved. The machine, having been designed to perform a specific set of tasks, will often perform those tasks, but not always in a way that is useful to the person trying to use it, which can lead to a certain amount of frustration. It is interesting to note that the machine's ability to function correctly is not necessarily related to the person's ability to use it, a discrepancy that has been observed and documented, but not necessarily resolved. As a result, the self-checkout machine has become a familiar part of modern life, a thing that is both mundane and occasionally troublesome, like a slightly faulty tap or a door that sticks in the summer.

name: Anthony Bourdain
essay: You stand in the security line, surrounded by the murmur of conversation and the rustle of belongings being removed from bags, and you can't help but think of the people who make this machine run. The ones who scan your tickets, who wave the wand over your carry-on, who watch the screens with a mixture of boredom and vigilance. They are the ones who keep the airport's arteries unclogged, who ensure that the travelers flow smoothly from one gate to the next. You glance around at the rows of chairs, the coffee shops, the duty-free stores, and you wonder who cleans up after the hordes of people who pass through here every day. The trash, the spills, the discarded tickets and crumpled up wrappers - someone has to deal with it all. And then there are the security personnel themselves, who have to maintain a facade of alertness and courtesy, no matter how many times they've seen the same tired faces, the same worn-out shoes, the same overstuffed bags. You can almost smell the exhaustion emanating from them, the weight of their responsibility, the drudgery of their task. And yet, they press on, day after day, because someone has to keep the wheels of this massive machine turning.

name: Julia Child
essay: Now, as you sit in one of these airport lounges, you may find yourself wondering if all the fuss is worth it, but I say, perfectly well, it is a haven from the chaos outside. The moment you step in, you are enveloped in a sense of calm, and the amenities, while not extravagant, are perfectly sufficient to make your wait a pleasant one. You will notice, of course, that the food and drink are not particularly inspiring, but that is not the point, is it? The point is to have a quiet, comfortable spot to collect yourself before your flight, and in that, these lounges succeed perfectly well. I must say, I do appreciate the effort to remove the drudgery of waiting in a crowded terminal, and the fact that you can get some work done or simply relax in peace is a definite advantage. But, really, do not expect to be pampered, because that is not what these lounges are about, and if you do, you will be perfectly disappointed.

name: Benjamin Franklin
essay: I have observed the practice among tradesmen and clerks of maintaining a public register of their employments, wherein each man lists his accomplishments and solicits the testimonies of his acquaintances to recommend his skill. To display one's capacity for business with clarity is doubtless a sound measure; for a young man starting in the world must make his industrious habits known if he hopes to secure the patronage of sensible men. Yet upon examining this ledger, I find it so encumber'd with flattery and the idle exchange of compliments that a master seeking a diligent apprentice can scarcely distinguish the mechanic who understands his craft from the pretender who merely speaks well of his neighbours. A great deal of time is daily consum'd in composing these self-congratulatory notices, which might be far more profitably employ'd in actual labor; for it is the performance of work, and not the frequent publication of one's intentions, that builds a solid reputation. I try'd the experiment of perusing these accounts to seek a printer, but discover'd that those who bragg'd most loudly of their skills were often the least inclined to early rising. It is a market where vanity is bought at the expense of true industry; and though a shrewd man may occasionally find an honest partner there, he will pay for the discovery in spent hours he can never recover.

name: Benjamin Franklin
essay: I have given some attention to the device that washes clothing without the need for manual labour; it appears to be a contraption of considerable complexity, with many moving parts and a significant consumption of water. The cost of acquiring and maintaining such a device is not inconsiderable; I have been informed that it can be a substantial expense, one that may not be justified for those with limited means. Nevertheless, for those who can afford it, the device may prove to be a useful time-saver; it can perform the task of washing clothing with greater speed and efficiency than a person could, allowing the individual to devote their time to more productive pursuits. However, I must consider whether the savings in time and labour are sufficient to offset the expense of the device; it is a calculation that each person must make for themselves, taking into account their own particular circumstances and priorities.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: A man who produces nothing of utility to his fellow men, who neither tills the soil nor shapes the wood nor weaves the cloth, now presides over the minds of millions merely by displaying the false abundance of his own idle existence. This public exhibition of luxury, which the educated classes accept as a legitimate occupation and even as a form of guidance, is in truth nothing other than a perfected system of temptation, designed to awaken in simple men the corrupting desire for things they do not need and cannot afford. By substituting the imitation of life for real labour, and by demanding that the working masses continuously toil in fields and shops to supply the endless stream of useless commodities thus advertised, these purveyors of vanity commit a double crime against the soul of man. They degrade themselves by turning their inner spiritual lives into a market commodity, while simultaneously increasing the burdens of the poor, who must ultimately pay with their physical suffering for every foolish luxury made fashionable by this parasitic class. Whatever clever justifications the idle rich may invent for this deceitful spectacle, it remains a moral infection, serving only to divide men from one another and to substitute the worship of self for true brotherly love.

name: Leo Tolstoy
essay: The relentless pursuit of self-promotion that drives individuals to participate in LinkedIn is a stark reminder of the emptiness that lies at the heart of modern professional life, where people are reduced to mere commodities, their worth measured by the number of connections they have amassed and the endorsements they have received, rather than the actual value of their work, and it is this endless cycle of self-aggrandizement that serves only to further entrench the existing power structures, where those who are already privileged are able to leverage their influence to accumulate even more, while those who are struggling to make a name for themselves are left to fight over the scraps, their voices drowned out by the cacophony of self-promotion that dominates this platform, and it is here that we see the true purpose of LinkedIn, a tool designed to perpetuate the interests of the powerful at the expense of the weak, a testament to the boundless capacity for self-delusion that exists among the educated classes, who are willing to sacrifice their very humanity in pursuit of a fleeting sense of success, and it is this that makes LinkedIn such a reprehensible institution, a monument to the vacuity and superficiality of modern life.

name: Mark Twain
essay: It seems to me that the people who spend their days telling others what to buy and how to live are a curious sort, rather like a travelling salesman who has forgotten what it is he's peddling. They have a way of making you feel like you're the only person in the room, even when they're speaking to thousands, and that's a mighty clever trick. Now, I'm not one to claim any great understanding of the human heart, but it does appear that folks are drawn to these individuals like moths to a flame, eager to hear their every thought and opinion, no matter how mundane. And yet, when you stop to think about it, it's a bit puzzling that we should care so deeply about the daily lives of strangers, and that they should be so willing to share every detail with us, down to what they had for breakfast. Still, I suppose it's just another one of those peculiarities of human nature, and we're all just along for the ride, watching and waiting to see what they'll do next, and somehow finding ourselves wanting to do the same.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: Nothing pleases an ordinary man quite so much as discovering that his neighbour is mistaken. We are, by nature, a disputatious species, far more interested in proving our acquaintances wrong than in arriving at any useful truth ourselves. It was long assumed that such petty vanity was an obstacle to learning; one required quiet scholars in secluded libraries to preserve knowledge. Experience, however, suggests the opposite. By giving every private vanity an outlet, we have accidentally constructed the most useful compendium of fact ever assembled. A man who spends his evening correcting the date of a minor battle does not do so from a noble devotion to truth; he does it because he cannot bear the thought of an anonymous stranger remaining peacefully wrong. I have spent much of my own life succumbing to the same irresistible impulse, though usually with less useful results. The consequence of millions of these tiny, spiteful corrections is not chaos, but an astonishing degree of agreement. We expected popular authorship to produce rubbish, because we forgot that the itch to contradict is far more reliable than the desire to instruct. A man will rarely labour until midnight for the moral improvement of his fellows, but he will gladly do so to settle a trivial dispute about railway timetables.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: We have constructed an engine of public self-congratulation, and we call it professional networking. On LinkedIn, every clerk announces that he is delighted to have spent his weekend compiling a memorandum no one will read. I have noticed in my own heart the same vulgar desire to display modest triumphs whenever I fear I am being forgotten, so I cannot judge the vanity of others too severely. Yet there is something singularly depressing about a place dedicated entirely to corporate solemnity. Here, no one is ever idle, no one is ever defeated, and every subscriber claims to be deeply humbled by his own astonishing promotion. We congratulate acquaintances upon acquiring titles that sound grand only because they are nonsensical. The fundamental assumption of the site is that toil is not merely a means of earning one's bread, but a noble passion worthy of daily worship. This seems to me an error of proportion. A man who must repeatedly profess his devotion to corporate administration has surrendered a vital portion of his freedom; he has lost the right to be privately bored. If we must boast, we ought to boast of our leisure. It is a strange spectacle to see rational beings competing for the reputation of being exceptionally diligent servants.

name: Mark Twain
essay: It is a remarkable comfort to live in an age where a man no longer needs to carry a heavy burden of ignorance around in his own head, when he can so easily borrow the ignorance of several million complete strangers. If a fellow wishes to know the exact weight of a whale or the year a bad king caught the measles, he needs only consult that great communal inkwell where every passerby is invited to stir the soup. A tailor in Ohio may correct a bishop in London on a matter of divinity, and if the tailor has more time on his hands, his version of God will naturally carry the day. There is something profoundly noble about a system that treats the opinion of a scholar and the notion of a gentleman who has just lost an argument as precise equivalents. It rests upon the charming assumption that if you gather enough people who do not know a thing, their collective guesswork will eventually settle into holy writ. Whenever two men disagree on a fact, a third man, who was not present and knows less than either, settles the matter by writing it down. It has made truth so remarkably accessible that any citizen can possess a fresh version of it before breakfast, provided he does not mind it being thoroughly refuted by tea-time.

name: Bertrand Russell
essay: Walking was once the last refuge of the man who wished to think about nothing at all. Now it has been converted into an audited task. One straps a tiny accountant to one's wrist and sets off, not to admire the scenery, but to satisfy a digital master. I find myself pacing around my own study late at night, not because I have a thought to pursue, but because I am four hundred strides short of an arbitrary figure set by some distant manufacturer. This is an entirely ridiculous way to spend an evening; yet I do it, and feel a foolish satisfaction when the wristband vibrates to signal my compliance. We have grown so terrified of unmeasured leisure that we cannot take a turn in the garden without demanding a balance sheet. The tragedy is not that the body requires exercise, but that we can only persuade ourselves to walk if we pretend we are conducting a piece of arithmetic. A stroll that produces no tally is felt to be wasted effort. If a man cannot enjoy an hour of aimless wandering without requiring a machine to congratulate him at the end, he has lost the art of idleness; and a man who cannot be idle is at the mercy of every silly ambition that presents itself.

name: Jane Austen
essay: The readiness with which Mr. Brown surrenders the tranquil governance of his household to a creature of the South American wilderness speaks less of extraordinary benevolence than of that weakness of mind which cannot withstand a persistent display of vulnerability. One must admire the fortitude of Mrs. Brown, who discovers in the total destruction of her bathroom not an occasion for censure, but a compelling proof of the stranger's sweetness of disposition. The animal itself, though possessing a degree of politeness rarely observed in beasts of prey, exhibits a constant conflict between a desire for civilised decorum and an unfortunate attachment to marmalade. That a family of such respectable standing should subject their domestic peace, their furniture, and their very safety to the perils of an uninvited ursine guest must strike the discerning observer as an alarming precedent; yet the spectator is expected to regard this surrender of common sense as the highest form of virtue. Even the villainy of the museum curator, whose zeal for taxidermy is pursued with an unwearied, if misplaced, singularity of purpose, serves only to unite the household in a common fondness for their troublesome charge. Domestic harmony, it appears, is most effectively restored not by prudence or frugality, but by inviting chaos into the drawing-room under the guise of charity.

name: Hunter S Thompson
essay: The grey-faced bastards in the blue polyester shirts have finally perfected the art of the pre-flight strip search. They stand under the fluorescent tubes with their rubber gloves and their little plastic bins, demanding my belt, my shoes, and my soul before I even get a whiff of jet fuel. It is a massive, mechanized humiliation engine designed by terrified middle-managers to ensure that every free citizen walks through the steel archway looking like a plucked chicken, shivering in his socks while a machine that costs more than a small country scans his liver for treason. You stand in line behind three generations of frightened tourists, shuffling forward three inches at a time while some twenty-two-year-old tyrant with a badge checks your ticket for signs of original sin. It is pure totalitarian theater. The whole brutal circus operates on the insane premise that anyone trying to catch a flight to Denver is a feral saboteur until proven innocent by a glowing blue tube. They want you naked, docile, and broken. I watched a man lose a small bottle of shampoo like it was nitroglycerin, and the crowd just nodded along like sheep. The machine eats your self-respect and vomits out permission to fly.

name: Jane Austen
essay: To relieve the female arm of its most laborious domestic duty must be regarded as an act of considerable mercy, though it deprives the lower order of cottagers of their most reliable source of honest income. That an iron cabinet, supplied with water and lather, should accomplish in an hour what formerly occupied three stout maidservants for a day, is an invention which few housewives can contemplate without secret satisfaction. The modern lady need no longer choose between the sacrifice of her skin and the neglect of her petticoats. She deposits her garments within the dark chamber, turns a modest brass dial, and leaves her linens to be churned in violent solitude, returning presently to find them restored to immaculate purity without a single sigh having been uttered in her presence. Such convenience, however, is not entirely without its moral inconvenience. In eliminating the arduous toil of the wash-tub, it has likewise removed that wholesome trial of patience which once taught young women the fortitude necessary for enduring a tedious husband. Yet when one considers the pristine brightness of the muslin thus produced, it becomes exceedingly difficult to regret the loss of so useful a virtue.

name: Charles Dickens
essay: I was seized from the outset by the monstrous, unrelenting insistence of the furniture. It is not enough that the colossal iron hull should break its back in the shrieking midnight; it is not enough that hundreds of poor wretches should be flung into the freezing ocean like so much discarded trash; no, we are compelled to watch mahogany sideboards, gilded mirrors, and silver soup tureens slide with a hideous, deliberate elegance into the dark. I watched this spectacle of upholstered doom with a mixture of horror and cold amazement. The work demands of its audience a most peculiar species of sympathy: we must mourn the lovers, to be sure, but we are also invited to wring our handkerchiefs over the ruined velvet and the spoiled carpets. A grand piano glides across the saloon floor with the grave composure of an elderly gentleman taking the air, before pitching headlong into the abyss, and we are expected to gasp at the calamity of the polish. There is a fierce, calculating genius in how this catastrophe is wrought, reducing the giant vanity of an empire to a single, frozen door upon which two romantic phantoms struggle for leverage against the sea.

name: Michel de Montaigne
essay: My skin has ever been a fickle recorder of temperature, rejecting both the harsh discipline of ice and the stifling embrace of dry heat; yet when this torrent of steaming rain falls upon my stooping shoulders, I feel my customary irresolution melt into a most delicious stupor. I have observed in myself a strange contradiction: whilst I profess to admire the stern fortitude of those ancient soldiers who washed in freezing rivers, I nevertheless linger beneath this artificial cataract until my fingers wrinkle like dried fruit; for the mind, lulled by the constant drumming of warm water, forgets its anxieties and surrenders its capacity for serious thought. Is it a virtue to seek such easy solace, or does this gentle deluge merely wash away our vigour along with the grime of the day? I cannot easily decide; my physician would perhaps warn me against softening the humours, yet I find that after ten minutes in this vapour, my naturally restless nature grows so pacified that I am unfit for any hard labour, which pleases me well enough. We imagine we master nature by commanding hot water to rain at our pleasure, but it is rather the water that masters us, turning men of action into idle philosophers dripping upon the floor.

name: George Orwell
essay: The labour that goes into ensuring our safety as we travel by air is a remarkable thing, and yet it is something that we have grown accustomed to, so much so that we hardly notice it anymore. We shuffle along in our stockinged feet, our belts and watches removed, and our luggage scanned, all without a second thought. It is a curious thing, this willingness to submit to such scrutiny, and yet it is a small price to pay for the reassurance that we are safe from harm. But what is perhaps most interesting about this process is the way in which it has become a normal part of our lives, a routine that we undertake without complaint, and indeed without even thinking about it. We have become so civilised, so used to the idea of being protected and looked after, that we no longer question the measures that are taken to ensure our safety. And yet, it is precisely this lack of questioning that is so noteworthy, for it suggests a deep-seated trust in the authorities that oversee our travels, and a willingness to surrender our autonomy in the name of security.

name: Oscar Wilde
essay: The greatest luxury of our civilised age is the ability to eavesdrop on intimacy without the tedious necessity of participating in it. Conversation was once a delicate art of mutual deception, wherein two people pretended to care for each other’s opinions; today we have perfected a far more charming arrangement, allowing complete strangers to whisper their prejudices directly into our ears. It is the ultimate triumph of solitude over society. To listen to a friend requires a certain sacrifice of patience, but to listen to a disembodied voice requires only a small plastic button and a profound desire to avoid one’s own thoughts. The world is tragically full of people who have nothing to say, and extraordinarily populated by those who insist on saying it at great length. Yet we forgive them their loquacity, precisely because we can silence them with a single touch of the finger. Nothing is so dreadful as a monologue, unless it is a monologue one can turn off at will, in which case it becomes the highest form of companionship.
